title: Graph Algorithms for Networking I Quiz
description: 20 questions covering graph network modeling, BFS hop-count, DFS cycle detection, and Dijkstra's algorithm.

questions.question: When modeling a telecommunications network as a graph G = (V, E), what do the vertices V and edges E represent?

options.text: V represents IP addresses, E represents MAC addresses
V represents network nodes/routers, E represents physical or logical communication links
V represents application sockets, E represents TCP sequence numbers
V represents autonomous systems, E represents DNS servers

questions.explanation: In network graph theory, vertices represent routing nodes or switches, and edges represent communication links.

questions.question: How does Cisco OSPF calculate the edge weight (cost) of an interface by default?

options.text: Cost = 1 for all interfaces
Cost = Reference Bandwidth (10^8 bps) / Interface Bandwidth (bps)
Cost = Physical Cable Length in meters * 10
Cost = Current packet queue length

questions.explanation: OSPF uses inverse bandwidth: Cost = 100 Mbps / Interface Bandwidth in bps. Higher speed links produce lower costs.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Breadth-First Search (BFS) on an unweighted graph G = (V, E) using an adjacency list?

options.text: O(V + E)
O(E log V)
O(V log V)

questions.explanation: BFS enqueues each vertex at most once and inspects each edge once, yielding O(|V| + |E|) time complexity.

questions.question: Why is standard BFS insufficient for routing in modern heterogeneous networks?

options.text: BFS cannot find cycles in graphs
BFS computes shortest path strictly by hop count, ignoring link capacities, bandwidth, and latency
BFS cannot be implemented with a FIFO queue
BFS requires negative edge weights

questions.explanation: A 1-hop 56 kbps dialup link would be chosen by BFS over a 2-hop 100 Gbps fiber line because BFS treats all link costs as 1.

questions.question: In network topology exploration, how does Depth-First Search (DFS) detect routing loops using the three-color node marking algorithm?

options.text: When an edge points to a BLACK node
When an edge points to a GRAY node (currently on the recursion call stack)
When an edge points to a WHITE node
When all nodes become RED

questions.explanation: A directed edge pointing to a GRAY node represents a back-edge to an active ancestor on the recursion stack, formally proving a cycle.

questions.question: In a network graph, what is an 'articulation point' (cut-vertex)?

options.text: A router whose removal disconnects the remaining network graph into two or more components (Single Point of Failure)
A switch running Spanning Tree Protocol
A port running full-duplex Gigabit Ethernet
A leaf node with degree 1

questions.explanation: An articulation point is a critical network node whose failure partitions the graph, representing a single point of failure (SPOF).

questions.question: What is the foundational prerequisite condition required for Dijkstra's algorithm to guarantee an optimal shortest path?

options.text: The graph must be a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)
All edge weights must be strictly non-negative (w >= 0)
The graph must be complete
The number of vertices must equal the number of edges

questions.explanation: Dijkstra relies on the greedy property that extracting the minimum tentative distance node finalizes its optimal distance. This fails if negative weights exist.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm implemented with an Adjacency List and a Binary Min-Heap Priority Queue?

options.text: O((V + E) log V)
O(V * E)

questions.explanation: With a binary min-heap: extracting minimums takes O(V log V) and edge relaxations/pushes take O(E log V), totaling O((V + E) log V).

questions.question: In Dijkstra's algorithm, what does the edge relaxation step if dist[u] + w(u, v) < dist[v] accomplish?

options.text: It deletes edge (u, v) from the graph
It updates dist[v] to the cheaper path through u and sets predecessor[v] = u
It restarts the priority queue
It switches the network interface to promiscuous mode

questions.explanation: Relaxation tests whether passing through vertex u offers a shorter path to v than previously recorded, updating dist[v] and predecessor pointers.

questions.question: How does a router running OSPF translate Dijkstra's shortest path tree into its physical Forwarding Information Base (FIB)?

options.text: It stores the complete end-to-end path in every packet header
It traces predecessor pointers back from each destination to determine the local outgoing interface and next-hop neighbor IP
It broadcasts the entire tree to the ISP
It copies all routes into the DNS cache

questions.explanation: Hop-by-hop forwarding only requires knowing the immediate Next Hop and physical egress interface for each destination prefix.

questions.question: Which of the following real-world routing protocols utilize Dijkstra's algorithm as their internal path computation engine? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)
IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System)
RIP (Routing Information Protocol)
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)

questions.explanation: OSPF and IS-IS are Link-State protocols that execute Dijkstra's algorithm. RIP uses Bellman-Ford, and BGP uses Path Vector.

questions.question: In a 3-node graph with links A-B (cost 4), A-C (cost 2), and C-B (cost 1), what is the shortest path cost from source A to destination B computed by Dijkstra?

options.text: 4 (direct path A-B)
3 (path A-C-B)
5 (path A-B-C)
1 (path C-B)

questions.explanation: A -> C (cost 2) + C -> B (cost 1) = cost 3, which is lower than direct link A -> B (cost 4).

questions.question: What data structure in Dijkstra's algorithm holds the vertices whose shortest path has NOT yet been permanently finalized?

options.text: FIFO Queue
LIFO Stack
Priority Queue (Min-Heap)
Circular Buffer

questions.explanation: A Min-Heap priority queue allows efficient O(log V) extraction of the vertex with the minimum tentative distance.

questions.question: What is the difference between propagation delay and transmission delay when calculating edge weights in a network graph?

options.text: Propagation delay depends on packet length; transmission delay depends on cable length
Propagation delay is the physical time for a signal to travel the cable distance (d / v); transmission delay is the time to push bits onto the wire (L / R)
They are identical terms for latency
Transmission delay occurs only on wireless networks

questions.explanation: Propagation delay = distance / speed of light (approx 200,000 km/s in fiber). Transmission delay = Packet size / Link bandwidth.

questions.question: If an edge weight represents latency, and two paths exist: Path 1 (1 hop, 50ms) and Path 2 (3 hops, 15ms total), which path will Dijkstra choose?

options.text: Path 1, because it has fewer hops
Path 2, because its cumulative edge weight (15ms) is lower
It will randomly alternate between both
It will fail because Path 2 has 3 hops

questions.explanation: Dijkstra minimizes the sum of edge weights along the path, selecting Path 2 (15ms) over Path 1 (50ms).

questions.question: What is asymmetric routing in real-world computer networks?

options.text: Packets from A to B travel via a different physical path than returning packets from B to A
Packets travel faster than the speed of light
A router uses IPv4 for outgoing and IPv6 for incoming packets
Half-duplex Ethernet communication

questions.explanation: Asymmetric routing occurs when outbound and inbound traffic take different network paths due to differing ISP policies or hot-potato routing.

questions.question: In a graph with |V| = 1000 routers and |E| = 3000 links, why is Dijkstra with a binary heap much faster than naive Dijkstra with an array?

options.text: Binary heap runs in O(V + E log V) ≈ 3.3x10^4 ops vs. array O(V^2) = 1,000,000 ops
Binary heap requires no memory
Array implementation cannot handle positive numbers
Binary heap converts graphs into trees

questions.explanation: For sparse graphs (E << V^2), a min-heap scales with O(E log V), which is orders of magnitude faster than searching an array in O(V^2).

questions.question: Can Dijkstra's algorithm detect if a destination node is completely unreachable from the source?

options.text: No, it enters an infinite loop
Yes, unreachable nodes retain their initial tentative distance of infinity (float('inf'))
No, it returns cost 0 for unreachable nodes
It raises a Segmentation Fault

questions.explanation: Vertices in disconnected components are never extracted or relaxed; their recorded distance remains infinity.

questions.question: Which of the following metrics can be legally used as edge weights in Dijkstra's algorithm? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: Propagation delay in milliseconds (non-negative)
Hop count (w = 1 for each link)
Financial transit cost in dollars per gigabyte (non-negative)
Negative packet rebate incentives (w < 0)

questions.explanation: Any non-negative cost metric is valid for Dijkstra. Negative metrics (D) violate Dijkstra's greedy invariant and cause incorrect results.

questions.question: How does an SDN (Software-Defined Networking) controller use graph algorithms compared to traditional distributed routers?

options.text: The centralized SDN controller maintains a global view of all switches and computes optimal paths centrally, downloading flow rules to switches
SDN controllers disable all graph algorithms
SDN switches run Dijkstra independently on each port
SDN switches only support BFS

questions.explanation: In SDN, the control plane is centralized. The SDN controller computes shortest paths globally and installs flow forwarding entries directly into switch TCAMs via OpenFlow.
